Sports and fitness turf on Poinciana's village-sized lots

Sports and fitness turf in Poinciana, a bocce lane, an agility strip or a home-gym sled track, gets quoted per job once the layout and length are known, not from a flat square-foot rate, since a narrow lane costs differently than an equivalent patch of lawn. Which village a lot sits in matters more here than almost anywhere else in the build, since Solivita rules out an on-lot court entirely.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Solivita's rule is worth stating plainly: courts aren't allowed

Solivita's Architectural Review Requirements state plainly that "tennis courts, play courts and game courts are not permitted within Lots," which takes a fixed sports surface off the table for any individual villa there regardless of size or design. What a Solivita homeowner usually ends up asking for instead is something narrower, a sled or agility strip along a side yard rather than a marked court, and even that scaled-down request still needs the same ARC sign-off as any other exterior change.

A standard APV village lot has more room to work with, not more approval to skip

Outside Solivita, the DCB's Design Control Board Criteria don't ban a court the way Solivita's do, but they still box in where one can go: an ancillary structure has to sit at least 10 feet off the rear property line and seven and a half feet off the side, and a basketball hoop is capped at one per household in one of three approved locations. A bocce lane or a compact agility strip fits inside those same setbacks along a side or rear fence line on a standard village lot, more room than Solivita allows but still a bounded footprint rather than an open one.

Working post footings into a batting cage's base plan

A batting cage's netting frame needs its corner and mid-span posts set into their own footings within the same base a Poinciana yard's turf sits on, and those footings have to go in before the surrounding washed rock gets compacted around them, not after. Loose fill packed in close to a footing after the fact settles unevenly over time and can let a post lean, which slackens the netting it holds. Planning footing locations against the base layout at the start keeps the compacted rock and the posts settling together rather than working against each other later.

Testing the bare base before any turf goes on top

Before turf ever gets rolled out on a Poinciana bocce court or batting cage base, the compacted rock gets tested the way the finished surface will actually be used: rolling a ball down the bare base or bouncing one off it to feel for a soft spot or an uneven stretch that would otherwise hide under the turf until someone plays on it. Catching an inconsistency at this stage means reworking exposed rock, which is a far smaller job than pulling installed turf back up to fix a base problem discovered after the fact.

Say you have a 12 by 35 ft side yard

Say you have a Village 8 side yard, 12 feet wide and running 35 feet along the fence line, currently mowed grass that holds water for a day or two after any real summer storm. A sled and agility lane built into that strip clears the DCB's seven-and-a-half-foot side setback with room to spare, and gets priced from a site visit rather than a set range, since the base depth needed for repeated sled traffic drives labor more than the lane's square footage does. The same layout on a Solivita villa would never clear as a fixed lane, though a shorter fitness strip could still go in front of the ARC.

Where a sled lane and a bocce court land on the same lifespan scale

Synthetic turf generally lasts ten to twenty years depending on UV stabilization, traffic, and infill, and within a single Poinciana property, a home-gym sled lane and a backyard bocce court can land at very different points on that same scale. A sled lane sees maximum-intensity loading nearly every time it's used, which pushes it toward the shorter end regardless of how often that actually happens, while a bocce court used for casual weekend games sees lighter, less frequent wear and tends to hold up closer to the higher end of the range over the same span of years.

Flatwoods drainage matters more on a longer, narrower surface

A sled lane or an agility strip runs long and narrow compared with a lawn section, which means a bigger share of its footprint sits right at whatever grade the crew builds into the base. On Poinciana's flatwoods soil, that grade has to carry water off a run twenty or thirty feet long just as reliably as it clears a compact square of lawn, or the low end of the lane holds water the rest of the yard sheds fine. Our glossary of turf terms is worth checking when comparing pile height and backing options between a sports lane and a plain lawn.

The shade a bocce court wants is exactly what the drip-line rule limits

A bocce court under oak canopy plays more comfortably through a Poinciana afternoon than one baking in full sun all day, which makes the shaded spot under a mature tree tempting to build on, but the same drip-line rule applies here as anywhere else: no turf inside the root zone without a certified arborist's letter confirming the excavation for a curb and base won't harm the tree. The appeal of shade for a long outdoor match is not a reason to skip that step, and getting the letter before digging is the only way to use that shaded footprint at all.

Clearing debris from a batting cage's frame track after a storm

Leaves and small branches that collect where a Poinciana batting cage's netting frame meets the turf can work into the base track along the bottom rail after a storm, and left there, that debris interferes with the same drainage the surrounding turf relies on and can catch on the net's bottom edge during use. A quick clear-out along that specific track, not just a general glance at the lane itself, keeps both the drainage and the frame's netting moving the way they're supposed to.

Questions people ask

Can I put in a home sports court in Solivita?

No. Solivita's Architectural Review Requirements rule out tennis, play and game courts on any individual lot regardless of size or design; a smaller fitness lane can still go before the ARC as a landscaping request.

How is sports turf priced in Poinciana?

Each lane or court gets its own site-visit quote instead of a square-foot rate, since length, layout and the base depth a specific surface needs vary more here than they do between two similarly sized lawns.
